newsitem.title: JAPAN: SWIMMING-NOW PAN PACIFIC CHAMPIONS LOOK TO EUROPE.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-NOW PAN PACIFIC CHAMPIONS LOOK TO EUROPE.

text.p: American Jenny Thompson, gold medal swim star of the Pan Pacific championships, is now looking to Europe for a form guide for next year's world showdown in Australia.
Thompson is among competitors and coaches at the Pan Pacific meeting that ended on Wednesday who will follow with keen interest the European championships starting next week in Seville, Spain.
Thompson's five golds here included the women's 100 metres freestyle title in 54.82, better than the 54.88 German Sandra Volker swam to take the silver medal at last year's Atlanta Olympics.
The American said how well Volker performed in Spain would tell her how much work she had to do to prepare for the world championships in Perth next January.
"Volker has been swimming very well, so it will be interesting to see her times," said Thompson, who has won five Olympic golds.
"The (European) results will certainly let us know where we stand," head U.S. women's coach John Collins said.
"There are some big holes in some of the events and we want to see how they are filled."
The coach of Costa Rica's Claudia Poll said he was hoping to see some fast times out of Seville, especially from Ireland's Michelle Smith, who won three golds in Atlanta.
"We want someone in Europe to have times close to Claudia," said coach Francisco Rivas. "We need Michelle Smith and other swimmers to push Claudia."

Poll took both the 200 and 400 freestyle races in Fukuoka, with her 200 time of 1:57.48 the third-best ever, and her 400 time of 4:06.56 was the best since Janet Evans of the United States swam a 4:05.85 in 1993.
Smith's Atlanta golds included the 400 freestyle, while Poll took the 200 event.
Others will be watching to see the times of Russian sprint star Alexander Popov, even though his coach said on Wednesday that Popov was not concerned about other swimmers.

"Nobody pushes Alex, he swims as fast as he needs to win," said Gennadi Touretski, who was in Fukuoka because he is now based in Australia where, in addition to training Popov, he coaches rising Australian talent Michael Klim.
The times of another Russian, Denis Pankratov, who holds the world record of 52.27 in the 100 butterfly, will be watched by Neil Walker of the United States.
"There are a lot of great swimmers in Europe and Pankratov is one of them," Walker said. "I just hope I can stay close to him."
